questions.question: What is the name of the main law that protects your personal data in the European Union?
options: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
European Privacy Act (EPA)
Digital Rights Directive (DRD)
Universal Data Law (UDL)
questions.hint: Look for the acronym that stands for General Data Protection Regulation.

questions.question: If you ask a company to show you what personal data they have collected about you, how must they respond under EU law?
options: They must provide it to you, usually within one month.
They can ignore you unless you are a paying customer.
They only have to show you if you suspect them of a crime.
They are legally forbidden from showing you your own data.
questions.hint: Companies are on a strict timeline once you make this request.

questions.question: Why do websites constantly ask you to 'accept cookies' when you visit them?
options: To test your internet connection speed.
To prove you are a human and not a robot.
Because EU law requires them to get your clear permission before they can track your online behavior and personal data.
Because it is required to make the website load faster on your browser.
questions.hint: It has to do with getting your consent before monitoring what you do on their site.

questions.question: Under EU law, you have the 'right to be forgotten'. What does this mean?
options: The government must erase all public records of your birth.
Companies must delete your personal data if you ask them to and they no longer have a valid reason to keep it.
You can legally change your name online without notifying your bank.
Social media platforms must automatically hide your old posts after 5 years.
questions.hint: It is about your right to ask an organization to erase your personal information when it's no longer necessary.

questions.question: If you want to know exactly what personal information a company (like a social media app or a store) has collected about you, what can you do?
options: You have the right to request a free copy of your data from them at any time.
You have to hire a lawyer to force them to reveal it.
You cannot find out, as that information is considered a protected company secret.
You must pay a standard fee to the EU government to access it.
questions.hint: The 'Right of Access' means you don't need a lawyer or money to see what information a company holds on you.

questions.question: What happens if you choose to click 'Reject All' on a website's cookie banner?
options: The website is legally allowed to block you from reading its content.
Your internet provider will slow down your connection.
The website should still function normally, but they cannot track your behavior for targeted advertising.
Your computer will automatically delete all saved passwords for that site.
questions.hint: Rejecting these trackers protects your privacy without breaking the main features of the website.

questions.question: What does the 'right to data portability' allow you to do as an EU resident?
options: Travel freely across EU borders with your laptop without it being searched.
Store your data on a portable USB drive instead of the cloud.
Delete all your personal data from the internet permanently with one click.
Receive your personal data from a company in a common format so you can easily move it to a competitor's service.
questions.hint: Think about 'porting' or transferring your phone number from one provider to another, but applied to your personal data.

questions.question: If an app or company gets hacked and your sensitive personal data is stolen, what obligation do they have to you under EU law?
options: They must inform you without undue delay if the breach poses a high risk to your privacy and security.
They are only required to tell the police; they do not have to inform the affected users.
They must automatically pay you a mandatory fine of at least 1,000 Euros.
They have up to one full year to publicly announce the hack on their website.
questions.hint: Think about your right to protect yourself when your sensitive information is actively at risk.
